newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe calls on supporters to close ranks.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe calls on supporters to close ranks.

text.p: Prime Minister Alain Juppe called on his fractious conservative coalition to close ranks behind him on Friday as French unemployment leaped to a post-war record.

Buoyed by a highly unusual call for order from President Jacques Chirac, Juppe told parliamentarians of his Gaullist RPR party that unity was crucial if the centre-right was to retain power in a general election due in March 1998.
"Jacques Chirac needs a united majority and government to carry out his mission. We owe this to France which must not fall back into socialism," he told MPs in the port of Le Havre.
Before Juppe spoke, the Labour Ministry announced the number of jobless had jumped by 39,500 in August -- the biggest monthly increase in over three years -- to reach a record 12.6 percent.
Under fire from within his own party for his economic policies, Juppe admitted the rise in unemployment was bad news but implored his critics to be patient.
He said he was open to proposals, but had not received any suggestions for an alternative policy to budget austerity and income tax cuts to revive growth and consumer spending.
"There can be no employment without growth, and no growth without sound finances," the deeply unpopular Juppe said.
"Reform takes time, tenacity, perseverance...We need time for reform to bear fruit and for the harvest to come," he said.

Deputies hailed his address as a display of authority. But his main party critics, ex-premier Edouard Balladur, National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin and former interior minister Charles Pasqua had all left the meeting before he spoke.
It was the second time in two days that the conservative premier had had to plead for coalition unity.

The centre-right won power in a landslide in 1993, but worsening unemployment and a stagnating economy have badly hurt the standing of Chirac and Juppe as they strive to cut budget deficit to fulfill the Maastricht criteria for joining the European single currency in 1999.
Chirac stepped in to defend his prime minister on Thursday, telephoning floor leader Michel Pericard to ask him to tell the RPR parliamentarians any attack on Juppe was an attack on himself.

His intervention in coalition affairs was highly unusual since France's Fifth Republic constitution places the head of state above party politics. Most commentators said it was a sign of Juppe's weakness.

It came after Balladur, a defeated presidential contender, hit out at Juppe's moves to stiffen anti-racism laws and add an element of proportional representation to France's first-past-the-post parliamentary election system.

The pro-government daily Le Figaro said Juppe had pressed Chirac to restore order in the RPR, threatening to boycott the party's annual parliamentary conference, and even, according to some unidentified Gaullist deputies, to resign.

An official source in Chirac's office called the report "pure fabrication", saying Juppe had not seen or called Chirac, and it was the president who took the initiative of telephoning Pericard to voice indignation at the coalition sniping.
The source said Chirac's call to order was aimed at the entire centre-right coalition, whose junior partner, the Union for French Democracy (UDF), also criticised Juppe this week.
